stem: Before starting pegloticase for refractory gout, which test is essential and why?

options.B: HLA-B*58:01 — severe skin reactions
options.D: TPMT — myelosuppression
options.E: Serum magnesium — arrhythmia

why: Pegloticase (uricase) has boxed warnings for anaphylaxis, infusion reactions, and hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency. Premedicate, stop other urate-lowering drugs and monitor serum urate.

whys.A: Not required.
whys.D: That is azathioprine.
whys.E: Not a pegloticase screen.

takeaway: Pegloticase: test G6PD first.
discriminator: Each gout drug has its own pre-test: HLA-B*58:01 vs. G6PD.

stem: A 70-year-old with severe osteoporosis and prior pelvic radiation for cervical cancer is considered for an anabolic drug. Which is the problem?

options.B: Raloxifene is the anabolic of choice
options.C: Teriparatide must be given IV yearly
options.D: Prior skeletal radiation rules out teriparatide
options.E: Teriparatide is limited to a 6-month lifetime course

why: Teriparatide (PTH 1–34 analog, 20 mcg SC daily, 2-year lifetime limit) is contraindicated with Paget disease, prior skeletal radiation, bone metastases, hypercalcemia and open epiphyses; follow with an antiresorptive to keep gains.

whys.A: Choice depends on risk and contraindications.
whys.C: It is 20 mcg SC daily.
whys.E: Lifetime limit is 2 years.

takeaway: Teriparatide: no prior skeletal radiation, Paget, bone mets.
discriminator: Know the anabolic's exclusion list.

stem: A patient's first gout flare settled 3 weeks ago; urate is 9.2 mg/dL and he has had 3 flares this year. Allopurinol is started. What should accompany it for the first months?

options.A: Probenecid during the first flare that occurs
options.B: Nothing; allopurinol prevents flares from day one
options.D: Stop allopurinol if a flare occurs
options.E: Colchicine 0.6 mg once or twice daily

why: Urate-lowering therapy mobilizes urate and triggers flares at initiation; colchicine 0.6 mg once or twice daily is used as prophylaxis while titrating. If a flare occurs, treat it and continue the allopurinol.

whys.A: Not started during an acute flare.
whys.C: That is a toxic misuse of the flare regimen.
whys.D: Continue it; treat the flare.

takeaway: Starting ULT → colchicine prophylaxis; don't stop ULT for a flare.
discriminator: Flare drug vs. urate-lowering drug: different jobs, same patient.

stem: A patient on etanercept and methotrexate calls with a temperature of 38.6 °C and a productive cough, and wants a live vaccine before a trip next month. What is the best advice?

options.B: Continue etanercept; give the live vaccine now
options.D: Switch to abatacept plus etanercept
options.E: Hold it, get seen now, skip the live vaccine

why: Immunosuppression raises infection risk: fever is infection until proven otherwise. Live vaccines are avoided on biologic or immunosuppressive therapy; update vaccines before starting. Abatacept is never combined with TNF inhibitors.

whys.A: Adds immunosuppression during infection.
whys.B: Live vaccines are avoided on biologics.
whys.C: Fever on a biologic is infection until proven otherwise.
whys.D: Abatacept is not combined with TNF inhibitors.

takeaway: Fever on a biologic → evaluate now; no live vaccines.
discriminator: Three safety rules in one call.

stem: A 74-year-old on sertraline and tramadol has an acute back spasm. She drives and lives alone. Which relaxant is the poorest choice?

options.B: Cyclobenzaprine
options.C: Baclofen at a low starting dose
options.D: Metaxalone
options.E: Non-drug care with acetaminophen

why: Cyclobenzaprine is tricyclic-related: anticholinergic, sedating, on the Beers list for older adults, and risks serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and tramadol.

whys.A: Less sedating than cyclobenzaprine.
whys.C: Spasticity drug; no serotonin interaction.
whys.D: Relatively favorable sedation profile.
whys.E: A reasonable start.

takeaway: Cyclobenzaprine: Beers list, anticholinergic, serotonin syndrome with SSRI/tramadol.
discriminator: Age + serotonergic drugs both point away from cyclobenzaprine.

stem: A 63-year-old with knee osteoarthritis had a bleeding gastric ulcer last year and a sulfonamide allergy. Acetaminophen alone is not enough. Which option best fits?

options.B: Topical diclofenac gel on the knee
options.D: Celecoxib 200 mg once daily
options.E: Ketorolac 10 mg every 6 hours for a month

why: Topical NSAIDs give local relief with much lower systemic exposure — a fit for knee OA when oral NSAIDs are risky. Celecoxib would spare the stomach but is contraindicated with sulfonamide allergy.

whys.A: Prior GI bleed: oral nonselective NSAID is high risk.
whys.C: Prior bleed: high GI risk with oral NSAIDs.
whys.D: Sulfonamide allergy is a contraindication.
whys.E: Limited to 5 days; GI bleeding boxed warning.

takeaway: Prior GI bleed + sulfa allergy → topical diclofenac, not celecoxib.
discriminator: Two filters remove two different drugs.

stem: A patient's daughter calls: her mother has been taking her 'weekly' methotrexate 15 mg every morning for 6 days and now has mouth sores and a low white count. Which response is correct?

options.B: Hold one week, then resume the same daily dosing
options.C: Leucovorin rescue plus CBC, liver, kidney labs
options.D: Give extra folic acid and continue daily
options.E: Switch to a TNF inhibitor the same day

why: Methotrexate is 7.5–25 mg ONCE WEEKLY with folic acid 1 mg daily. Daily dosing by mistake causes severe toxicity (mucositis, myelosuppression); leucovorin is the rescue, with CBC, liver and creatinine monitoring.

whys.A: Daily dosing by mistake causes severe toxicity.
whys.D: Daily dosing is the error; leucovorin is the rescue.
whys.E: Infection risk while myelosuppressed; manage toxicity first.

takeaway: Methotrexate daily by mistake → leucovorin rescue.
discriminator: Folic acid prevents; leucovorin rescues.

stem: A 52-year-old of Han Chinese ancestry with recurrent gout and an eGFR of 45 is starting allopurinol. Which plan is best?

options.A: HLA-B*58:01 test, low start, urate goal < 6
options.B: Titrate to urate under 8 mg/dL
options.D: Start during the current flare to stop it
options.E: Skip flare prophylaxis; flares won't happen

why: Allopurinol: start 50–100 mg daily and titrate every 2–5 weeks to serum urate under 6 mg/dL; reduce dose in renal impairment; HLA-B*58:01 carriers (higher in some Asian ancestries) are at higher risk of severe hypersensitivity; flares at initiation need prophylaxis.

whys.C: Higher-risk ancestry; start low in renal impairment.
whys.D: Start after the flare settles.
whys.E: Flares at initiation are expected.

takeaway: Allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01, start low, urate < 6, cover flares.
discriminator: A Unit 1 gene test applied to a Unit 2 drug.

stem: A patient with osteoporosis has taken denosumab for 6 years and wants to stop all treatment. Compared with stopping a bisphosphonate after 6 years, what is different?

options.A: Both should simply be stopped after 5 years
options.B: No difference; both keep working for years
options.D: Stopping a bisphosphonate causes the rebound
options.E: Denosumab protects longer because it is an antibody

why: Bisphosphonates bind bone and are retained for months to years (hence a drug holiday). Denosumab does not deposit in bone: stopping or missing doses causes a surge of resorption and multiple vertebral fractures — transition to a bisphosphonate.

whys.A: Denosumab needs a transition plan.
whys.D: Bisphosphonate is retained in bone for months to years.
whys.E: Its effect reverses when stopped.

takeaway: Stopping denosumab → rebound fractures; bisphosphonate lingers in bone.
discriminator: Compare reversibility, not just mechanism.

stem: A 55-year-old who drinks 4–5 beers nightly has knee osteoarthritis and stage 3 CKD. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Which analgesic plan fits best?

options.B: Acetaminophen, capped at 2–3 g/day
options.C: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food
options.D: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 2 weeks
options.E: Celecoxib 200 mg daily to spare the stomach

why: With CKD and an anticoagulant, NSAIDs carry the highest combined renal and bleeding risk, so acetaminophen is the safer first-line choice — but chronic alcohol use (or liver disease) lowers its maximum from 3–4 g/day to 2–3 g/day.

whys.A: Chronic alcohol use lowers the daily maximum to 2–3 g.
whys.C: NSAID + CKD + anticoagulant: kidney and bleeding risk.
whys.D: Same NSAID red flags: CKD and an anticoagulant.
whys.E: Still a renal risk, and CV risk, in CKD.

takeaway: Alcohol or liver disease → acetaminophen max 2–3 g/day.
discriminator: Pick the right drug and the right dose for the same patient.

stem: A patient with RA and recurrent diverticulitis is being considered for tocilizumab. Which concern and monitoring plan fit?

options.A: GI perforation; monitor CBC, LFTs, lipids
options.B: Retinal toxicity; baseline and annual eye exams
options.D: Orange urine; no monitoring needed
options.E: Teratogenicity; cholestyramine washout

why: Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist): infection, elevated liver enzymes, neutropenia, hyperlipidemia and rare GI perforation — caution with diverticulitis; monitor CBC, liver enzymes and lipids.

whys.C: A TNF-inhibitor concern.
whys.D: That is sulfasalazine.
whys.E: That is leflunomide.

takeaway: Tocilizumab: diverticulitis caution; CBC, LFTs, lipids.
discriminator: Match each DMARD to its own monitoring.

stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis and stage 4 CKD takes baclofen 20 mg three times daily and is newly drowsy and confused. What is the most likely explanation and response?

options.B: Stop it abruptly today
options.D: CYP1A2 interaction; stop ciprofloxacin
options.E: Renal accumulation; reduce the dose gradually

why: Baclofen is renally cleared: caution in renal impairment (sedation, confusion, coma in overdose). Never stop abruptly — withdrawal causes seizures, hyperthermia and rebound spasticity — so taper.

whys.A: Caution in renal impairment — it accumulates.
whys.B: Abrupt stop: seizures, hyperthermia, rebound spasticity.
whys.C: These are excess-drug signs, not withdrawal.
whys.D: That is tizanidine's interaction.

takeaway: Baclofen: renal caution; taper, never stop abruptly.
discriminator: Fix accumulation without causing withdrawal.

stem: A 66-year-old with stage 4 CKD takes clarithromycin for pneumonia and now has an acute gout flare in the knee. Which flare treatment is best?

options.A: Colchicine 1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg an hour later
options.B: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily
options.D: A short course of prednisone
options.E: Start allopurinol 300 mg today

why: Colchicine is contraindicated with severe renal impairment plus CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors like clarithromycin (narrow therapeutic window, fatal toxicity). Corticosteroids are the taught alternative when NSAIDs or colchicine are contraindicated, including CKD.

whys.A: Severe renal impairment + CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitor: contraindicated.
whys.B: NSAIDs are a poor fit in stage 4 CKD.
whys.C: eGFR under 30 and acute flare are contraindications.
whys.E: Don't start urate-lowering therapy for a flare.

takeaway: CKD + clarithromycin + flare → corticosteroid.
discriminator: Eliminate by contraindication: colchicine (CYP3A4), NSAID (CKD), probenecid (eGFR, flare).

stem: A 29-year-old man with RA on sulfasalazine says his urine is orange and he and his partner have not conceived. Which interpretation is right?

options.B: Infertility is permanent; stop all DMARDs
options.C: Orange urine signals hepatotoxicity, so stop it today
options.D: Expected sulfasalazine effects; sperm count recovers
options.E: These suggest G6PD deficiency

why: Sulfasalazine adverse effects include orange urine and reversible oligospermia, plus nausea, rash, myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity (monitor CBC and liver tests).

whys.A: He is on sulfasalazine.
whys.C: Orange urine is a harmless known effect.
whys.E: G6PD raises hemolysis risk; not these findings.

takeaway: Sulfasalazine: orange urine, reversible oligospermia.
discriminator: Benign-but-alarming effects are common exam bait.

stem: Three days after coronary artery bypass grafting, a patient asks for something stronger than acetaminophen. Which statement about NSAIDs is correct here?

options.A: Celecoxib is safe because it spares COX-1
options.B: Ketorolac is preferred for up to 5 days
options.C: All are contraindicated in this setting
options.D: Ibuprofen is fine at OTC doses
options.E: Any NSAID is fine with a PPI added

why: The drug profiles list the CABG setting as a contraindication for ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, ketorolac (perioperative CABG) and celecoxib.

whys.A: CABG setting is a celecoxib contraindication too.
whys.B: The CABG setting is a contraindication.
whys.D: CABG setting is listed for ibuprofen.
whys.E: A PPI does not address the cardiovascular contraindication.

takeaway: CABG setting: no NSAIDs — selective or not.
discriminator: COX-2 selectivity protects the stomach, not the heart.

stem: A 78-year-old with osteoporosis has a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min. Which therapy best fits her kidney function?

options.B: Risedronate with extra water
options.D: Alendronate 10 mg daily instead of weekly
options.E: Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months, watching calcium

why: Alendronate and zoledronic acid are avoided when CrCl is below 35 mL/min. Denosumab is not renally cleared and can be used in advanced renal disease — watch for hypocalcemia.

whys.A: Avoid with CrCl below 35.
whys.C: Avoid with CrCl below 35.
whys.D: Same CrCl problem.

takeaway: CrCl < 35 → no bisphosphonate; denosumab (check calcium).
discriminator: Renal clearance decides between two antiresorptives.

stem: A 24-year-old arrives 10 hours after taking a large amount of acetaminophen at once. The lab says a level will take 3 hours. What is the best next step?

options.A: Start NAC now; don't wait for the level
options.B: Give NAC only if symptoms of liver failure appear
options.C: Wait for the level, then plot it on the nomogram
options.D: Give activated charcoal only and observe
options.E: Plot a level only if AST and ALT are high

why: NAC replenishes glutathione and works best early, ideally within 8 hours. When presentation is late or a level is unavailable and the ingestion is significant, start NAC without waiting.

whys.B: By then hepatocyte necrosis is established.
whys.C: Late presentation with a significant ingestion: don't delay NAC.
whys.D: NAC is the antidote; delay worsens liver injury.
whys.E: Normal early enzymes do not rule out toxicity.

takeaway: Late or unknown level + significant ingestion → start NAC now.
discriminator: The nomogram guides; it never delays the antidote.

stem: A 68-year-old is given ketorolac after an orthopedic procedure. Which plan follows the drug profile?

options.A: Use it to bridge until celecoxib starts working
options.B: Switch to oral after 5 days for 2 more weeks
options.C: Standard dose, since age doesn't matter
options.D: Reduced dose for age, and 5 days or less in total
options.E: 30 mg IV every 6 hours for 10 days

why: Ketorolac is for short-term moderately severe acute pain: total course 5 days or less (max 120 mg/day IV/IM), reduced dose at age 65+, with boxed warnings for GI bleeding, renal failure, bleeding and CV events.

whys.A: Not the indication; short-term acute pain only.
whys.B: The 5-day limit is the total course.
whys.C: Age 65+ needs a reduced dose.
whys.E: Course is limited to 5 days or less.

takeaway: Ketorolac: ≤ 5 days total; reduce dose at 65+.
discriminator: Potency comes with a hard stop.

stem: A 50-kg woman with mild RA takes hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and has a borderline-long QT on citalopram. Which change best follows the drug profile?

options.A: Stop eye exams since the dose is standard
options.B: Lower the dose to stay within 5 mg/kg/day
options.C: Raise to 600 mg for better RA control
options.D: Keep 400 mg; the maximum is per ideal weight
options.E: Add azithromycin to cover infection risk

why: Hydroxychloroquine: 200–400 mg daily, maximum 5 mg/kg/day actual body weight (here 250 mg). Retinal toxicity needs baseline and annual eye exams; caution with QT-prolonging drugs.

whys.A: Baseline and annual eye exams are needed.
whys.C: Exceeds the maximum and adds QT risk.
whys.D: The limit uses actual body weight: 400 mg = 8 mg/kg.
whys.E: Adds another QT-prolonging drug.

takeaway: HCQ max 5 mg/kg/day (actual weight); eye exams; QT caution.
discriminator: Do the arithmetic: 400 mg ÷ 50 kg = 8 mg/kg.

stem: A patient with RA who failed a TNF inhibitor is starting rituximab. Screening shows chronic hepatitis B. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: Faster RA response because of the infection
options.B: Only an infusion reaction, prevented by premedication
options.C: Risk of hepatitis B reactivation, a boxed warning
options.D: Lymphoma as the main risk at first infusion
options.E: No issue, since rituximab targets B cells only

why: Rituximab (anti-CD20) boxed warnings: infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation and PML. Screen hepatitis B first; premedicate with acetaminophen, an antihistamine and a steroid.

whys.A: No such effect.
whys.D: The boxed warnings are infusion reactions, HBV reactivation and PML.
whys.E: B-cell depletion is why hepatitis B reactivates.

takeaway: Rituximab: screen hepatitis B first.
discriminator: Deplete B cells, lose control of hepatitis B.

stem: A kidney-transplant patient on azathioprine had a myocardial infarction last year. She needs urate-lowering therapy. Which drug is the worst choice for her?

options.B: Febuxostat
options.C: Allopurinol with an azathioprine dose cut
options.D: Pegloticase, if gout becomes refractory
options.E: Colchicine for flare prophylaxis

why: Febuxostat is contraindicated with azathioprine or mercaptopurine and carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death — two strikes for this patient.

whys.A: Uricosuric; limited by eGFR, not by azathioprine.
whys.C: Usable with a major thiopurine dose reduction.
whys.D: Reserved for refractory gout; not ruled out by these findings.
whys.E: Prophylaxis, not a contraindicated pairing here.

takeaway: Febuxostat: no azathioprine; CV death boxed warning.
discriminator: One drug, two reasons to avoid it.

stem: An 80-kg patient develops malignant hyperthermia after sevoflurane and succinylcholine. What is the correct initial dantrolene dose?

options.B: 25 mg by mouth daily
options.C: 800 mg IV as a single first dose
options.D: 200 mg IV (2.5 mg/kg), repeated up to 10 mg/kg
options.E: Baclofen 20 mg by mouth

why: Dantrolene blocks RyR1 calcium release in muscle. MH: 2.5 mg/kg IV (80 kg → 200 mg), repeat up to 10 mg/kg. Oral use carries a hepatotoxicity boxed warning; caution with calcium channel blockers (IV).

whys.A: 1 mg/kg; under-dosed and not repeated.
whys.B: That is the oral spasticity start.
whys.C: 10 mg/kg is the ceiling, not the first dose.
whys.E: Central GABA-B agonist; not the MH drug.

takeaway: Dantrolene MH: 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeat to 10 mg/kg.
discriminator: Weight-based dose math at the bedside.

stem: A woman on raloxifene for osteoporosis is scheduled for knee replacement with several days of immobility. What is the key counseling point?

options.A: Stop raloxifene before the period of immobilization
options.B: Double the dose to protect the new joint
options.C: Hot flashes are the main surgical risk
options.D: Continue it; it protects against hip fracture
options.E: Switch to estrogen for surgery

why: Raloxifene (SERM): boxed warning for VTE and death from stroke; stop before prolonged immobilization. It reduces spine (not hip) fractures and lowers invasive breast cancer risk.

whys.C: VTE is the boxed warning.
whys.D: It protects the spine, not the hip.
whys.E: Not the taught plan.

takeaway: Raloxifene: VTE — stop before immobility.
discriminator: The boxed warning drives the peri-operative plan.

stem: A 46-year-old with RA not controlled on methotrexate has multiple sclerosis and NYHA class III heart failure. Which biologic choice is least appropriate?

options.B: Abatacept
options.D: Adalimumab
options.E: Continuing methotrexate alone

why: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab) are contraindicated with demyelinating disease and NYHA III–IV heart failure, besides active infection and untreated latent TB.

whys.A: Infection, lipids and liver; no demyelination contraindication.
whys.B: No demyelination or heart-failure contraindication listed (caution in COPD).
whys.C: Severe heart failure is listed — but not demyelinating disease.
whys.E: Not ideal, but not harmful in the same way.

takeaway: TNF inhibitor no-gos: demyelinating disease, NYHA III–IV HF, untreated TB.
discriminator: The patient's two comorbidities both point at the same class.

stem: A 70-year-old on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide, and lithium for bipolar disorder, starts daily naproxen for hip pain. Two weeks later he is confused and tremulous and his creatinine has risen. What best explains this?

options.B: Serotonin syndrome from naproxen
options.D: Lithium lowering naproxen clearance
options.E: Triple-whammy AKI raising lithium levels

why: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is the ‘triple whammy’ for AKI, and NSAIDs raise lithium levels — the falling kidney function drives lithium toxicity (confusion, tremor).

whys.A: Doesn't explain the timing with naproxen.
whys.C: The pattern is renal, with lithium accumulation.
whys.D: Reversed: NSAIDs raise lithium levels.

takeaway: NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic → AKI; NSAIDs ↑ lithium.
discriminator: One added drug, two interactions.

stem: A 31-year-old with RA has taken leflunomide for 2 years. She wants to become pregnant within the year. What is the most appropriate plan?

options.B: Continue it; it is safe in pregnancy
options.D: Halve the dose until delivery
options.E: Stop it the week she conceives

why: Leflunomide (DHODH inhibitor) carries boxed warnings for hepatotoxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity; cholestyramine washout removes it. Methotrexate is also contraindicated in pregnancy.

whys.C: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy.
whys.D: Any dose is teratogenic.
whys.E: It persists; washout is needed beforehand.

takeaway: Leflunomide + pregnancy plans → cholestyramine washout.
discriminator: Both RA anchors (methotrexate, leflunomide) are teratogenic.

stem: A patient on tizanidine for spasticity starts ciprofloxacin for a UTI. Two days later his BP is 84/50 and HR 48, and he is very drowsy. What happened?

options.B: Ciprofloxacin induced tizanidine metabolism
options.D: Serotonin syndrome from the combination
options.E: Urosepsis unrelated to the drugs

why: Tizanidine (central alpha-2 agonist) is contraindicated with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine): levels rise → hypotension, bradycardia, CNS depression. Check liver tests.

whys.C: No withdrawal story here.
whys.D: Not this pair; that is cyclobenzaprine.
whys.E: Bradycardia + sedation fit tizanidine excess.

takeaway: Tizanidine + ciprofloxacin/fluvoxamine → hypotension, bradycardia.
discriminator: Inhibitor raises the victim drug (Unit 1).

stem: The day after her first zoledronic acid infusion, a woman has fever, muscle aches and fatigue. Her calcium was replete beforehand. What is the best explanation?

options.B: Acute-phase (flu-like) reaction
options.D: Rebound bone resorption
options.E: Osteonecrosis of the jaw from the infusion

why: Zoledronic acid (IV yearly): flu-like acute-phase reaction, hypocalcemia, renal injury and ONJ; hydrate and replete calcium and vitamin D first; avoid with CrCl below 35.

whys.A: An oral bisphosphonate problem.
whys.C: A long-term risk, not day-1 fever.
whys.D: That follows stopping denosumab.
whys.E: Jaw necrosis is rare and not acute.

takeaway: Zoledronic acid: flu-like reaction after the first infusion.
discriminator: Timing (next day) points to the acute-phase reaction.

stem: A patient with RA on weekly methotrexate is started on probenecid for gout. Which effect should the clinician anticipate?

options.B: Lower methotrexate levels and RA flares
options.D: Lower penicillin levels if she needs one
options.E: Faster uric acid production

why: Probenecid (URAT1 inhibitor) raises levels of penicillins, methotrexate and NSAIDs; it also causes kidney stones (hydrate, alkalinize urine) and is avoided with eGFR under 30 or during a flare.

whys.A: Probenecid interacts at renal excretion.
whys.D: Probenecid raises penicillin levels.
whys.E: Uricosurics raise urate excretion.

takeaway: Probenecid ↑ penicillin, methotrexate, NSAID levels.
discriminator: Penicillin adjunct = the same mechanism that raises methotrexate.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with very high fracture risk had a stroke 7 months ago. Romosozumab is being discussed. What is the correct decision?

options.A: Use it with aspirin for protection
options.B: Use it monthly for 3 years
options.C: Use it since it is antiresorptive only
options.D: Use it; the stroke was over 6 months ago
options.E: Avoid: stroke within the past year

why: Romosozumab (sclerostin antibody) carries a boxed warning: contraindicated after MI or stroke within the past year. Given 210 mg SC monthly for one year, then an antiresorptive.

whys.A: Not taught; still contraindicated.
whys.B: Course is 12 months, then an antiresorptive.
whys.C: It builds bone (sclerostin antibody).
whys.D: The window is the past year.

takeaway: Romosozumab: no MI or stroke within 1 year.
discriminator: Check the clock on the cardiovascular event.
